subject: Biology
text: Distinguish between mitosis and meiosis with respect to: (a) number of divisions and (b) nature of daughter cells.
modelAnswer: (a) Mitosis involves one division producing 2 daughter cells. Meiosis involves two successive divisions (meiosis I and II) producing 4 daughter cells. (b) Mitosis produces diploid (2n) daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell. Meiosis produces haploid (n) daughter cells that are genetically variable (recombined).
keyPoints: Mitosis: 1 division → 2 diploid cells (identical to parent)
Meiosis: 2 divisions → 4 haploid cells (genetically variable)
Meiosis occurs in reproductive organs (gonads); mitosis in somatic cells

subject: Biology
text: Explain how each of the following factors affects the rate of transpiration: (a) Light intensity (b) Humidity (c) Wind speed.
modelAnswer: (a) Light: stomata open in light → more transpiration. High light intensity = high transpiration rate. (b) Humidity: high humidity → less concentration gradient between leaf air spaces and atmosphere → less transpiration. Low humidity → high transpiration. (c) Wind speed: wind removes water vapour from near leaf surface, maintaining concentration gradient → increases transpiration rate.
keyPoints: Light: stomata open → increases transpiration rate
High humidity: reduces gradient → reduces transpiration
Wind: removes vapour → maintains gradient → increases transpiration

subject: Biology
text: A colour-blind father and a carrier mother have children. Using a Punnett square, show the probability of their children being colour-blind. (Use X^B for normal, X^b for colour blind allele)
modelAnswer: Father: X^b Y (colour blind). Mother: X^B X^b (carrier). Cross: X^b Y × X^B X^b. Offspring: X^B X^b (carrier daughter, normal), X^b X^b (colour-blind daughter), X^B Y (normal son), X^b Y (colour-blind son). Probability: 25% carrier daughter, 25% colour-blind daughter, 25% normal son, 25% colour-blind son. 50% of all children are colour-blind.
keyPoints: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive
Carrier mother (X^BX^b) × colour-blind father (X^bY)
50% children colour-blind (all sons 50%, daughters 50%)

subject: Biology
text: Describe the structure of a nephron with reference to: (a) Bowman's capsule (b) Glomerulus (c) Renal tubule (one part).
modelAnswer: (a) Bowman's capsule: cup-shaped double-walled structure at the beginning of the nephron that surrounds the glomerulus. The filtrate from blood passes into its cavity. (b) Glomerulus: a knot of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule; blood is filtered here under pressure — small molecules (water, glucose, urea, salts) pass into capsule. (c) Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): follows Bowman's capsule; site of selective reabsorption — glucose, amino acids, water, salts are reabsorbed back into blood.
keyPoints: Bowman's capsule: cup-shaped; collects glomerular filtrate
Glomerulus: knot of capillaries; ultrafiltration occurs here
PCT: selective reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, salts, water

subject: Biology
text: Distinguish between sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. Give one effect of each on the heart.
modelAnswer: Sympathetic nervous system: prepares body for 'fight or flight' — accelerates heart rate, dilates pupils, constricts blood vessels. Effect on heart: increases heart rate. Parasympathetic nervous system: promotes 'rest and digest' — slows heart rate, constricts pupils, increases digestive activity. Effect on heart: decreases heart rate (slows it down). They have antagonistic effects on same organs.
keyPoints: Sympathetic: fight-or-flight; increases heart rate (tachycardia)
Parasympathetic: rest-and-digest; decreases heart rate (bradycardia)
Both innervate same organs but produce opposite effects

subject: Biology
text: Explain the light reactions of photosynthesis: (a) Where do they occur? (b) What are the products? (c) What is photolysis of water?
modelAnswer: (a) Light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes (grana) of chloroplasts. (b) Products: ATP (adenosine triphosphate), NADPH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate), and O2 (released from photolysis of water). (c) Photolysis of water: splitting of water molecules using light energy — 2H2O → 4H+ + 4e− + O2. Oxygen is released as a by-product; electrons are used to reduce NADP+ to NADPH.
keyPoints: Light reactions: thylakoid membranes (grana)
Products: ATP, NADPH, O2
Photolysis: 2H2O → 4H+ + 4e− + O2 (light energy used)

subject: Biology
text: In pea plants, the gene for seed colour: Yellow (Y) is dominant over Green (y). (a) What would be the phenotypic ratio in the offspring of a cross Yy × Yy? (b) What percentage of offspring will be pure-breeding yellow?
modelAnswer: (a) Yy × Yy cross: YY : Yy : yy = 1:2:1. Phenotypic ratio = 3 Yellow : 1 Green. (b) Pure-breeding yellow = YY = 1 out of 4 = 25% of offspring.
keyPoints: Yy × Yy → 1YY : 2Yy : 1yy
Phenotypic ratio: 3 Yellow : 1 Green
Pure-breeding yellow (YY) = 25% of offspring

subject: Biology
text: Trace the path of deoxygenated blood from the right atrium to the lungs and back to the left atrium.
modelAnswer: Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs (oxygenation occurs — CO2 released, O2 absorbed) → pulmonary veins → left atrium. This is pulmonary circulation. The pulmonary artery is the only artery that carries deoxygenated blood; pulmonary veins are the only veins that carry oxygenated blood.
keyPoints: Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs
In lungs: CO2 released, O2 absorbed (oxygenation)
Pulmonary veins (4) → left atrium; only veins carrying oxygenated blood

subject: Biology
text: Distinguish between hormones and enzymes with respect to: (a) chemical nature and (b) site of action.
modelAnswer: (a) Hormones: mostly proteins or steroids (lipid-derived), e.g., insulin is a protein, oestrogen is a steroid. Enzymes: all proteins (globular proteins). (b) Hormones: produced in endocrine glands and transported by blood to act on distant target organs (act away from site of production). Enzymes: act at the site where they are produced or secreted (locally) — mostly in digestive tract, cells, etc.
keyPoints: Hormones: proteins or steroids; act on distant target organs via blood
Enzymes: all proteins; act locally where produced/secreted
Hormones: non-catalytic messengers; Enzymes: biological catalysts

subject: Biology
text: Explain the mechanism of opening and closing of stomata.
modelAnswer: Opening: In light, guard cells absorb K+ ions actively → water potential decreases → water enters guard cells by osmosis → guard cells become turgid → bean-shaped guard cells bow outward (their thick inner wall pulls apart) → stoma opens. Closing: In darkness/water stress, K+ ions leave guard cells → water potential rises → water leaves by osmosis → guard cells become flaccid → stoma closes. Abscisic acid (ABA) promotes closure in drought.
keyPoints: Opening: K+ in → osmosis → guard cells turgid → stoma opens
Closing: K+ out → water loss → guard cells flaccid → stoma closes
Light triggers opening; ABA/darkness/water stress triggers closing

subject: Biology
text: A DNA strand has 200 base pairs. If thymine (T) is 20% of the total bases, calculate: (a) the number of thymine bases and (b) the number of adenine, guanine and cytosine bases.
modelAnswer: Total bases = 200 × 2 = 400 (double-stranded DNA). (a) T = 20% of 400 = 80 bases. By Chargaff's rule: A = T, so A = 80. (b) A = 80, T = 80, G + C = 400 − 160 = 240; G = C = 120 each.
keyPoints: 200 bp → 400 total bases (double-stranded)
T = 20% → T = 80; A = T = 80 (Chargaff's rule)

subject: Biology
text: Describe what happens during ventricular systole: (a) Which valves open and which close? (b) What is the effect on blood pressure?
modelAnswer: (a) During ventricular systole (ventricles contract): Atrioventricular (AV) valves — tricuspid and mitral (bicuspid) — close (preventing backflow into atria). Semilunar valves — pulmonary and aortic — open (allowing blood to be pumped out to lungs and body). (b) Blood pressure rises sharply as ventricles contract powerfully and eject blood into arteries. This is the systolic pressure (the higher reading in blood pressure, e.g., 120 in 120/80 mmHg).
keyPoints: Ventricular systole: AV valves CLOSE, semilunar valves OPEN
Blood ejected into pulmonary artery and aorta
Blood pressure peaks at systolic pressure (e.g., 120 mmHg)

subject: Biology
text: Why is urea considered the main nitrogenous waste in humans? How is it formed?
modelAnswer: Urea is less toxic than ammonia and can be stored temporarily in the body before elimination. It is soluble in water and can be concentrated in urine, requiring less water for excretion (unlike ammonia which needs large amounts of water). Formation: Amino acids undergo deamination in the liver → ammonia (NH3) is released. Ammonia is immediately converted to urea in the liver through the ornithine cycle (urea cycle): 2NH3 + CO2 → CO(NH2)2 + H2O.
keyPoints: Urea: less toxic than ammonia; can be concentrated → less water loss
Formed in liver by deamination + ornithine (urea) cycle
2NH3 + CO2 → CO(NH2)2 (urea) + H2O

subject: Biology
text: Explain the role of the following in photosynthesis: (a) Magnesium (b) Chlorophyll (c) Stomata.
modelAnswer: (a) Magnesium: essential micronutrient; forms the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule (Mg²⁺ at the centre of the porphyrin ring). Without Mg, plants cannot make chlorophyll → leaves turn yellow (chlorosis). (b) Chlorophyll: the green photosynthetic pigment that absorbs light energy (mainly red and blue wavelengths) and converts it to chemical energy. It is the primary pigment for photosynthesis. (c) Stomata: tiny pores on leaves through which CO2 enters and O2 exits; also site of most transpiration. Guard cells regulate opening/closing.
keyPoints: Mg: central atom of chlorophyll ring; deficiency → chlorosis
Chlorophyll: absorbs light (red+blue); converts to chemical energy
Stomata: CO2 entry, O2 exit; regulated by guard cells

subject: Biology
text: Define population education. State two measures to control population growth.
modelAnswer: Population education: a systematic study of population concepts and processes to help individuals understand and be responsible about population problems; it includes education about family planning, reproductive health, and sustainable development. Measures: (a) Raising the legal age of marriage (India: 18 for girls, 21 for boys). (b) Family planning programmes — promoting contraception. (c) Female education and empowerment. (d) Incentives for small families.
keyPoints: Population education: awareness of population issues + family planning
Legal age of marriage delayed → reduces birth rate
Female education + contraception = effective population control methods

subject: Biology
text: Distinguish between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition with one example each.
modelAnswer: Autotrophic nutrition: organisms prepare their own food from simple inorganic substances using an external energy source. Example: green plants (photosynthesis using sunlight, CO2, water). Heterotrophic nutrition: organisms cannot make their own food and depend on other organisms for nourishment. Example: humans, animals, fungi (consume organic material).
keyPoints: Autotrophic: self-feeding; green plants (photosynthesis)
Heterotrophic: other-feeding; animals, fungi
Autotrophs = producers; heterotrophs = consumers in food chain

subject: Biology
text: Describe the events that occur during metaphase of mitosis.
modelAnswer: During metaphase: (a) Chromosomes are at their maximum condensation and are shortest and thickest — most visible under microscope. (b) Chromosomes align at the equatorial plate (metaphase plate) — midway between the two poles of the cell. (c) Spindle fibres (from centrioles/poles) attach to the centromeres of each chromosome. (d) Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Chromosomes can be counted and studied (karyotyping done from metaphase cells).
keyPoints: Metaphase: chromosomes fully condensed, most visible
Chromosomes align at equatorial plate (metaphase plate)
Spindle fibres attach to centromeres; sister chromatids held together

subject: Biology
text: Describe the structure and function of the cerebellum.
modelAnswer: Structure: The cerebellum is the second largest part of the brain, located at the back of the skull below the cerebrum. It has two hemispheres with a folded cortex (folia). Function: coordinates muscular movement and maintains balance and posture; it receives sensory information about body position and adjusts muscular contractions to produce smooth, precise movements. Damage to cerebellum causes unsteady gait (ataxia).
keyPoints: Cerebellum: back of skull, below cerebrum; folded surface (folia)
Function: coordination of muscular movements
Maintains balance and posture; damage → ataxia (unsteady gait)

subject: Biology
text: State the site of fertilization in humans. Describe what happens to the fertilized egg (zygote) immediately after fertilization.
modelAnswer: Site: Fertilization normally occurs in the Fallopian tube (oviduct), usually in the outer third (ampulla region). After fertilization: the zygote (fertilized egg) immediately begins mitotic cell division (cleavage) as it travels down the Fallopian tube. It becomes a 2-cell → 4-cell → morula (16 cells) → blastocyst. The blastocyst reaches the uterus (after ~5-7 days) and implants into the endometrium (uterine wall).
keyPoints: Fertilization: Fallopian tube (outer third/ampulla)
Zygote undergoes cleavage (mitosis) while moving to uterus
Blastocyst implants in uterine endometrium ~5-7 days after fertilization

subject: Biology
text: Describe the structure of a villus in the small intestine. How is it adapted for absorption?
modelAnswer: Structure: Villi are finger-like projections of the mucosa of small intestine. Each villus contains blood capillaries and a lacteal (lymph capillary). Surface cells have microvilli (brush border). Adaptations: (a) Enormous surface area — millions of villi, each with microvilli. (b) Single-cell thick epithelium — short diffusion distance. (c) Rich blood supply — capillaries take glucose/amino acids directly to portal vein; lacteals absorb fatty acids/glycerol. (d) Lacteal for fat absorption. (e) Constant blood flow maintains concentration gradient.
keyPoints: Villus: finger-like, contains blood capillaries + lacteal
Adaptations: large surface area (microvilli), thin epithelium, rich blood supply
Glucose/amino acids → blood capillaries; Fatty acids → lacteal

subject: Biology
text: State two differences between urine and blood plasma with respect to: (a) composition and (b) glucose content.
modelAnswer: (a) Composition: Blood plasma contains proteins (albumin, globulin, fibrinogen), glucose, amino acids, hormones, urea, salts. Urine contains urea, uric acid, creatinine, salts (NaCl, KCl) — no proteins (too large to filter) and no glucose (normally reabsorbed). (b) Glucose: Blood plasma normally contains glucose (~80-120 mg/100 mL). Normal urine contains no glucose (all glucose is reabsorbed in PCT). Glucose in urine (glycosuria) indicates diabetes mellitus.
keyPoints: Plasma: has proteins, glucose, hormones, amino acids
Urine: no proteins, no glucose (normally); has urea, salts, creatinine
Glucose absent in urine: completely reabsorbed in PCT

subject: Biology
text: Give the source, one function, and the effect of hyposecretion (deficiency) for each: (a) Insulin (b) Thyroxine.
modelAnswer: (a) Insulin: Source: β-cells of islets of Langerhans in pancreas. Function: lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake of glucose by cells and glycogen synthesis in liver. Hyposecretion: Diabetes mellitus — high blood glucose (hyperglycaemia), glucose in urine, excessive thirst. (b) Thyroxine: Source: thyroid gland. Function: regulates basal metabolic rate (BMR), growth, and development. Hyposecretion: in children → Cretinism (stunted growth, mental retardation); in adults → Myxoedema (lethargy, weight gain, low BMR).
keyPoints: Insulin: pancreas β-cells; lowers glucose; deficiency → diabetes mellitus
Thyroxine: thyroid; regulates BMR; child deficiency → cretinism
Adult thyroxine deficiency → myxoedema (goitre if iodine deficiency)

subject: Biology
text: What is a reflex action? Describe the reflex arc with its components.
modelAnswer: Reflex action: a rapid, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thinking. It is controlled by the spinal cord (spinal reflex). Reflex arc components: Receptor (sense organ detects stimulus) → Afferent (sensory) neuron → Spinal cord (nerve centre/relay neuron) → Efferent (motor) neuron → Effector (muscle/gland → response). Example: withdrawing hand from hot object.
keyPoints: Reflex: automatic, involuntary response; controlled by spinal cord
Arc: Receptor → Sensory neuron → Spinal cord → Motor neuron → Effector
Bypasses brain for rapid response; brain learns of action later

subject: Biology
text: Define: (a) dominant allele (b) genotype (c) phenotype. Give an example for each.
modelAnswer: (a) Dominant allele: the allele that expresses itself (shows its effect) in the phenotype whether present in homozygous or heterozygous state. E.g., T (tall) is dominant over t (dwarf). (b) Genotype: the genetic constitution (actual alleles) of an organism, e.g., TT or Tt or tt. (c) Phenotype: the observable physical characteristic or trait expressed by an organism, e.g., 'tall' or 'dwarf'. Phenotype = genotype + environment.
keyPoints: Dominant allele: expressed in homozygous AND heterozygous state
Genotype: actual alleles present (e.g., TT, Tt, tt)
Phenotype: observable trait expressed (e.g., tall or dwarf)

subject: Biology
text: Describe the role of the liver in: (a) glucose regulation (b) protein metabolism (c) detoxification.
modelAnswer: (a) Glucose regulation: liver converts excess glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis) when blood glucose is high (after meals). It converts glycogen back to glucose (glycogenolysis) when blood glucose falls (fasting). This maintains blood glucose homeostasis. (b) Protein metabolism: liver deaminates excess amino acids → removes amino group → forms urea (excreted by kidneys). Also synthesises plasma proteins (albumin, globulin, fibrinogen). (c) Detoxification: liver converts toxic substances (alcohol, drugs, ammonia) to less toxic/insoluble forms for excretion. Kupffer cells destroy old RBCs and bacteria.
keyPoints: Glucose: glycogenesis (excess→glycogen) and glycogenolysis (glycogen→glucose)
Protein: deamination → urea; synthesises albumin, globulin, fibrinogen
Detoxification: converts alcohol/drugs/ammonia to safe forms; Kupffer cells

subject: Biology
text: Describe the events in prophase of mitosis. Why is it the longest phase?
modelAnswer: Prophase is the longest phase of mitosis. Events: (a) Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes (each chromosome = 2 sister chromatids joined at centromere). (b) Nucleolus disappears. (c) Nuclear membrane breaks down (at late prophase). (d) Spindle fibres (mitotic spindle) begin to form from centrioles which move to opposite poles. It is the longest phase because chromosome condensation (coiling and shortening) is a complex, time-consuming process; the nuclear membrane dissolution and spindle formation also require time.
keyPoints: Chromatin condenses → visible chromosomes (2 chromatids each)
Nucleolus disappears; nuclear membrane breaks down
Spindle formation begins; centrioles migrate to poles

subject: Biology
text: (a) Define the law of limiting factors in photosynthesis (Blackman's Law). (b) State three factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: (a) Blackman's Law (Law of Limiting Factors): When a process is governed by a number of factors, the rate of that process is limited by the factor present in minimum amount (or at its minimum value). The rate of photosynthesis is determined by the factor in least supply. (b) Factors that can limit photosynthesis: (i) Light intensity, (ii) Carbon dioxide concentration, (iii) Temperature, (iv) Water availability, (v) Chlorophyll content.
keyPoints: Blackman's Law: rate controlled by limiting factor (in least supply)
Limiting factors: light intensity, CO2 concentration, temperature
Only one factor is limiting at any given time

subject: Biology
text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of a neuron. Name any three structural parts.
modelAnswer: A neuron consists of: (a) Cell body (soma): contains the nucleus and cytoplasm; metabolic centre of the neuron. (b) Dendrites: short branching processes that receive impulses from other neurons and pass them to the cell body. (c) Axon: long single projection that carries impulses away from the cell body to other neurons or effectors. (d) Myelin sheath: fatty insulating layer around some axons, speeding up transmission. (e) Nodes of Ranvier: gaps in myelin sheath. (f) Axon terminals (synaptic knobs): end of axon; release neurotransmitters.
keyPoints: Cell body: nucleus + cytoplasm; dendrites: receive impulses
Axon: carries impulses away from cell body (single long fibre)
Myelin sheath: insulates axon; Nodes of Ranvier: gaps in sheath

subject: Biology
text: Explain Mendel's Law of Dominance with an example from his pea plant experiments.
modelAnswer: Law of Dominance: when two organisms homozygous for contrasting alleles of a character are crossed (P1 generation), only one trait (dominant) appears in the F1 generation. The other trait (recessive) disappears in F1 but reappears in F2 in the ratio 3:1. Example: Tall (TT) × Dwarf (tt) → All F1 Tall (Tt). In F1, Tall is dominant, Dwarf is recessive. Cross F1 × F1: Tt × Tt → TT:Tt:tt = 1:2:1 (phenotype 3 Tall : 1 Dwarf). The recessive 'dwarf' reappears in F2.
keyPoints: Law of Dominance: only dominant trait appears in F1
TT × tt → all Tt (tall only in F1)
F1 × F1: 3 tall : 1 dwarf in F2; recessive reappears

subject: Biology
text: Explain the role of the kidney in osmoregulation. What happens to water reabsorption when blood becomes too concentrated?
modelAnswer: Kidneys regulate the water and ion content of blood (osmoregulation). When blood becomes too concentrated (low water potential): (a) Hypothalamus detects this → signals the posterior pituitary gland to release ADH (antidiuretic hormone/vasopressin). (b) ADH acts on the collecting duct and distal convoluted tubule of nephrons → makes them more permeable to water → more water is reabsorbed back into blood → less urine produced (concentrated urine). When blood is too dilute, less ADH is released → less water reabsorption → more dilute, copious urine.
keyPoints: Concentrated blood → hypothalamus signals → more ADH released
ADH → collecting duct more permeable to water → more water reabsorbed
Result: less urine produced (concentrated); less ADH → more dilute urine

subject: Biology
text: Describe the structure and function of the aorta. What are the two main branches it divides into?
modelAnswer: The aorta is the largest artery in the body, arising from the left ventricle. Structure: thick muscular elastic walls to withstand high pressure; large lumen; has the aortic valve (semilunar valve) at its base. Function: carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to all parts of the body (except lungs). It arches over the heart (arch of aorta) giving off branches to head, neck, arms, then descends as the descending aorta. Main branches: (a) Coronary arteries (to heart muscle itself), (b) Carotid arteries (to head/brain), (c) Subclavian arteries (to arms), and eventually bifurcates into iliac arteries (to legs/pelvis).
keyPoints: Aorta: largest artery; from left ventricle; thick elastic wall
Carries oxygenated blood to all body parts
Main divisions: coronary, carotid, subclavian → iliac arteries

subject: Biology
text: Explain the cohesion-tension theory of water transport in plants.
modelAnswer: The cohesion-tension theory explains how water moves from roots to leaves: (a) Transpiration from leaf cells creates tension (negative pressure / low water potential) in leaf mesophyll. (b) This tension is transmitted down through the water column in xylem vessels. (c) Cohesion (attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonding) keeps the water column continuous and unbroken. (d) Tension pulls water up from roots through xylem (wick effect). (e) Water enters roots from soil by osmosis as root cells have lower water potential.
keyPoints: Transpiration → tension/negative pressure in xylem
Cohesion (H-bonding) keeps water column continuous
Tension pulls water up from soil → roots → xylem → leaves

subject: Biology
text: Describe the menstrual cycle briefly. What is the significance of the luteal phase?
modelAnswer: The menstrual cycle (average 28 days): (a) Menstrual phase (Day 1-5): shedding of endometrium lining as menstrual blood — occurs when pregnancy doesn't happen. (b) Follicular phase (Day 1-13): FSH stimulates development of Graafian follicle in ovary; estrogen causes endometrium to thicken. (c) Ovulation (Day 14): LH surge triggers release of egg (ovum) from Graafian follicle. (d) Luteal phase (Day 15-28): ruptured follicle becomes corpus luteum; secretes progesterone + estrogen — thickens endometrium to prepare for implantation. Significance of luteal phase: progesterone maintains uterine lining, preparing it for implantation of fertilized egg. If no fertilization, corpus luteum degenerates → progesterone drops → menstruation begins.
keyPoints: Day 1-5: menstruation; Day 1-13: follicular (FSH, estrogen)
Day 14: ovulation (LH surge); Day 15-28: luteal (corpus luteum, progesterone)
Luteal phase: progesterone prepares endometrium for implantation

subject: Biology
text: What is the role of bile in digestion? Where is bile produced and stored?
modelAnswer: Bile is produced in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the duodenum when food enters. Role of bile: (a) Emulsification of fats — bile salts break large fat droplets into smaller ones (emulsification), increasing surface area for lipase action. (b) Neutralizes acid chyme from stomach — bile is alkaline (pH ~8), providing optimum pH for intestinal enzymes. (c) Bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin from broken-down hemoglobin) give faeces its colour.
keyPoints: Produced: liver; stored: gall bladder; released into duodenum
Emulsification: breaks fat into droplets → increases surface area for lipase
Neutralizes acid chyme; bile pigments colour faeces

subject: Biology
text: State the source, hormone produced, and one effect of hyposecretion for: (a) Adrenal cortex (b) Pancreatic alpha cells.
modelAnswer: (a) Adrenal cortex: Source — adrenal glands (cortex part, above kidneys). Hormone — corticosteroids (cortisol/glucocorticoids + mineralocorticoids). Hyposecretion — Addison's disease: low blood pressure, fatigue, skin darkening, low blood sugar, electrolyte imbalance. (b) Pancreatic alpha cells: Source — islets of Langerhans, alpha cells. Hormone — glucagon. Hyposecretion — hypoglycaemia (dangerously low blood glucose) as glucagon normally raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis in liver.
keyPoints: Adrenal cortex: cortisol/mineralocorticoids; deficiency → Addison's disease
Alpha cells (pancreas): glucagon; raises blood glucose (glycogenolysis)
Glucagon deficiency → hypoglycaemia
